content: Hyaluronan synthase 1 (HAS1) is an enzyme in humans that is encoded by the HAS1 gene. Hyaluronan, also known as hyaluronic acid (HA), is a high molecular weight, unbranched polysaccharide that is synthesized by a wide range of organisms, from bacteria to mammals. It is a key component of the extracellular matrix. The structure of HA consists of alternating residues of glucuronic acid and N-acetylglucosamine, which are linked together by beta-1,3 and beta-1,4 glycosidic bonds. HA is synthesized by a membrane-bound synthase located on the inner surface of the plasma membrane. The HA chains are extruded into the extracellular space through an ABC transporter. HA serves multiple biological functions, including acting as a space-filling molecule, providing lubrication in joints, and forming a matrix that facilitates cell migration. During wound healing and tissue repair, HA is actively produced to create a framework that supports the ingrowth of blood vessels and fibroblasts. Alterations in serum concentrations of HA are associated with inflammatory and degenerative joint diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis. Furthermore, the interaction between HA and the leukocyte receptor CD44 plays a critical role in tissue-specific homing of leukocytes. Overexpression of HA receptors has been linked to tumor metastasis. HAS1 belongs to a newly identified vertebrate gene family that encodes putative hyaluronan synthases. The amino acid sequence of HAS1 shares significant homology with the hasA gene product of Streptococcus pyogenes, a glycosaminoglycan synthetase (DG42) from Xenopus laevis, and a recently described murine hyaluronan synthase.
